title: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war
description: The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.Finland
body: The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said. Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole."We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said. Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered. Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state. "A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson. Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America. As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons. But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good". And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

schema.headline: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war

title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
description: British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told th
body: British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us. "We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit."He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be."But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement."We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election."I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

schema.headline: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement

title: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford
description: Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford last month.Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Wes
body: Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford last month.Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.  Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.The pair appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.The court heard vans bearing the logo "Fuel2You" were spotted close to the base. In the early hours, the vans came across a Ministry of Defence Police cordon and re-routed to another location.Police arrived and arrested five men. They later revealed that one had called 999 and reported what was going on.During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, Essghir stood in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and confirmed his name and address.His charge relates to an alleged "reconnaissance mission" on 22 August, around a month before the Fairford incident. Abdulkarim is charged with helping with the plot.He appeared in court in a wheelchair wearing a checked shirt, jeans and a baseball cap. He confirmed his name and address.Both men are charged under the 2023 National Security Act.Essghir has been remanded in custody, while Abdulkarim has been granted bail with conditions including the surrender of his passport.The case will be next heard at the Old Bailey on 20 November.Essghir was one of five men arrested near the base on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. All five were released on police bail the following day, but Essghir was re-arrested on 20 October.A 25-year-old UK-Iranian national who was also re-arrested on that date on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service has now been released without charge. He remains on police bail after his initial arrest on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.The re-arrests in October led to detectives interviewing Abdulkarim.Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the release of the five men on police bail in September had raised significant questions and speculation about the investigation for members of the public.He stressed that tactics used by counter-terror police can appear "illogical" at times but said that "there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them"."In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I've announced today," he added.

schema.headline: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford

title: Venus Williams: Former world number one loses to Lilli Tagger at Guangzhou Open
description: Williams won six of her Grand Slam singles titles - plus 30 WTA tournaments - before Austria's Tagger was born in February 2008.Tagger's coach Frances
body: Williams won six of her Grand Slam singles titles - plus 30 WTA tournaments - before Austria's Tagger was born in February 2008.Tagger's coach Francesca Schiavone - the Italian former world number four who won the 2010 French Open - is the same age as Williams, and lost all eight meetings with the American during her playing career."When I saw the draw I was super excited and a bit nervous - I respect her a lot," said Tagger, who is 53rd in the world."It is funny she used to play with my coach. I would love to play at this age - I want to congratulate her."While the straight-set scoreline will embolden the critics, Williams did make Tagger - a rising talent who is predicted to have a bright future at the very top - work hard.However, the teenager proved far too good. The 2025 French Open girls' champion was superb on serve - dropping just seven service points and not facing a break point - while handling Williams' pace and crushing groundstrokes off both wings.Tagger broke her illustrious opponent's serve twice - for 1-0 and 5-2 leads - in two almost identical sets.At times, Williams was able to use her powerful serve to get out of trouble - fighting off 12 of 16 break points - and the veteran's trademark competitive spirit never wavered.But it was another example of how far behind the rest of the tour she now is.

schema.headline: Venus Williams: Former world number one loses to Lilli Tagger at Guangzhou Open

title: Formula 1 next engine regulations to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines
description: Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existi
body: Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existing rules.A proposal document sent by governing body the FIA to the six manufacturers in F1 outlines a framework for discussions on engines to be introduced in either 2030 or 2031.Multiple sources within F1 have provided BBC Sport with the details within the document.The plan, which comes after initial discussions with individual engine manufacturers on a one-to-one basis, proposes cheaper, lighter, simpler engines with a more visceral sound.However, the FIA has moved away from its initial proposal to return to naturally aspirated engines.The stated aim of the new rules is to introduce lighter, more responsive cars, increased emphasis on driver skill, relevant technologies, reduced cost, to make it easier for new manufacturers to enter F1 and to continue with the sport's commitment to reducing emissions.This comes after criticism of the new engines introduced this year for their complexity and the way their design and operation has diminished the driving challenge of some of F1's best corners.The proposal changes the previous stance of the FIA on naturally aspirated engines - president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially proposed a return of V10s at the start of last year and has more recently been pushing V8s.The addition of the turbo satisfies the need for the engines to be road-relevant, as well as increasing efficiency and requiring less fuel than a pure naturally aspirated engine.The published proposals can be seen as a kind of middle ground between Ben Sulayem's initial stance, the desire of at least some manufacturers to keep turbos and a significant hybrid element, and a recognition that the latest rules were flawed in concept and execution.The new engines will have none of the problems of energy starvation about which drivers have complained this season.Fernando Alonso has called F1 the "battery world championship" and described fast corners as "the charging station for the car", while Max Verstappen has described the new rules  as "Formula E on steroids" and anti-racing.Both have since tempered their criticisms having seen that the sport's bosses have listened to their comments on the engines and made immediate changes to the rules this year as well as started working towards a new direction in the future.The fundamental framework of the proposal for the new engine's architecture is said to be basically acceptable to all the manufacturers.However, the details around how the rules operate will need discussion.The document outlines two possible ways forward for the new rule set.One is aimed at minimising necessary adaptation - for example, a 2.1-litre V8 could be produced by simply adding two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre blocks and reducing the size of the turbo and MGU-K (hybrid motor).The other, more controversial, is to have an external manufacturer design and supply a baseline power-unit with a high degree of standardisation, on to which manufacturers could add a degree of customisation.However, insiders say the manufacturers are all aligned on wanting to design and build their own power-units and for engines to remain a performance differentiator.The companies who currently supply engines to F1 teams are Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi, Honda and Red Bull. Cadillac, which entered F1 this year with its own team, is planning to produce an engine to the new rules.There are two further arguments to steer away from the standardisation route:The first is that the reasons for it - to safeguard against manufacturers leaving the sport - is irrelevant as all six will be committed under the new rule set.The second is that the standardisation of electronics control units this season has led to a series of problems, such as at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia when cars were restricted to not much more than walking pace because of a software bug.The document outlines a proposal to cut the engine budget cap by 50% from the current level of $190m (£143m) per year.However, this is considered a starting point for discussions, while there are also concerns about providing a suitable glide path down to the new number to enable teams to manage the impact on workforces.Discussions around the budget cap also involve the need to balance ongoing development of the existing engines with design and construction of the new ones.That topic is interlinked with whether the new rules will come into force in 2030 or 2031.The existing contracts in F1 bind the FIA, teams and commercial rights holder together only until 2030.Ben Sulayem has previously threatened to introduce his own rules unilaterally in 2031.That threat appears to have receded and the process has been marked by a spirit of co-operation, which is expected to continue.An FIA spokesperson declined to comment on or discuss the document, pointing instead to an Instagram post published on Ben Sulayem's account outlining the aims and objectives of of the new rules., external It makes no mention of turbos or hybrid technology.The aim is for discussions over the next weeks to lead to a proposal that can be put to F1's legislative body, the FIA world council, in December.

schema.headline: Formula 1 next engine regulations to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines

title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
description: Image source, Reuters/HandoutImage caption, The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or waterByPaul KirbyEurope d
body: Image source, Reuters/HandoutImage caption, The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or waterByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorOlga Malchevska and Dan Johnsonin KyivUpdated 1 hour agoA ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.Figure caption, What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania TrumpThat was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearThe current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedIt is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there". He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports."Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

schema.headline: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say

title: Was the Ballon d'Or in London the most chaotic?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Ballon d'Or ceremony began at 20:45 GMT instead of 20:00 because of traffic issuesBySarah DawkinsBBC Spor
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Ballon d'Or ceremony began at 20:45 GMT instead of 20:00 because of traffic issuesBySarah DawkinsBBC Sport senior journalistUpdated 4 hours agoIt was the first time the Ballon d'Or had been held in London in its 70-year history, with organisers choosing the iconic London Palladium as the venue.Despite the perfect homecoming for Harry Kane on Monday night, the rest of the event was not plain sailing.Did the organisers give away the winners early or was it just a simple mix-up? Why was the ceremony delayed and why was the audience booing?BBC Sport assesses a chaotic night in central London.Traffic, delay and a rowdy audienceLondon traffic can cause issues on any day but unfortunately for the Ballon d'Or organisers, they chose to hold a major event just a stone's throw from Oxford Street on the same day the famous shopping area was made traffic-free.That, coupled with large crowds at the event entrance, meant significant numbers of guests were delayed and the start had to be pushed back by 45 minutes.Once it did get under way, a rowdy and boisterous audience sat through a ceremony that lasted nearly two and a half hours. On a number of occasions, hosts Kate Scott and Thierry Henry had to briefly pause proceedings while people shouted the names of players in the audience and there were several instances of booing during commercial breaks.After Kane and Alexia Putellas had been crowned the winners in the two main categories, they then spoke to the world's media in separate press conferences.Journalists were able to put questions to Putellas but only men were selected to ask Kane a question, with several female journalists having their attempts seemingly ignored.The Ballon d'Or team has since apologised.Figure caption, Was this the most chaotic Ballon d'Or yet?Clashes with policeHundreds of people gathered outside the London Palladium to try to get a glimpse of the biggest stars in football on the red carpet. A security perimeter of metal fencing and barricades had been erected to try to keep those without a ticket out.But the BBC Sport team witnessed those barriers being scaled, broken and ripped down and several people being evicted by security after making their way through.The atmosphere at times was tense, with footage on social media appearing to show fans clashing with security and police.A Metropolitan Police spokesperson told BBC Sport that officers were requested to help "after concerns were raised about crowd behaviour and the potential for a breach of the peace"."A Section 35 dispersal order was authorised at 19:49 GMT and was in place until 04:00 on Tuesday, 27 October," a statement read."Officers cleared the crowd, who began throwing scaffolding clips and bricks towards police. No officers were injured. "Later in the evening, officers dealt with a relatively small number of individuals who had climbed a neighbouring building."It added that two arrests were made - one for breaching the dispersal order and another for affray and violent disorder.Website blunderThe confusion and chaos began hours before the ceremony had even started, after the official Ballon d'Or website published an article declaring Kane as the winner of the men's award.Further digging revealed similar articles had been published about some of the other favourites to win the men's and women's awards, including Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe and London City Lionesses' Putellas.Was it a genuine mistake? Or a case of trying to divert people's attention from the initial Kane announcement? Which of course turned out to be true.A Ballon d'Or spokesperson told BBC Sport last night they were "inadvertently published online"."These articles had been prepared for all nominees and should in no way be considered as an indication of the final results or rankings," the spokesperson said.The Ballon d'Or official social media accounts also mixed up the names of two of the women's nominees, congratulating 'Alexia Bonmati' on her victory. The post was later deleted.

schema.headline: Was the Ballon d'Or in London the most chaotic?

title: Michael Carrick: Why Man Utd are sticking with under-pressure manager - for now
description: When Michael Carrick disappeared down the tunnel after Manchester United's loss to Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the support from fans for a
body: When Michael Carrick disappeared down the tunnel after Manchester United's loss to Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the support from fans for a legendary player turned to hostility and anger at the current squad.The atmosphere afterwards was said to be emotional.Carrick was the last to leave the stadium and, as usual, patiently posed for selfies and signed shirts for the fans who remained on what had been a foul day weather-wise, and an awful one on the pitch.Asked in his post-match news conference if he expected to be in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea, Carrick said: "I'm not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I'm carrying on as normal."Few felt that was sustainable. Even Carrick's coaching team wondered whether they would survive.And yet, that is what has happened.United have decided Carrick and his players will have the chance to turn the present situation around. No timescale has been put on this, but Carrick will be in charge at Chelsea, with his team 16th in the table.They have a crucial Champions League match against Roma three days later, then a Premier League encounter with in-form Aston Villa before a two-week international break.No-one from Manchester United is saying so, but that would be the most obvious time to decide if a change of coach is required.On Monday morning, when it was widely anticipated an announcement terminating Carrick's tenure would be made, a senior figure at United said calmness and a clear head would be needed to navigate the turbulence around Old Trafford.Carrick had been treading water since the crushing 4-1 defeat at Como on 21 October - one of the worst European nights in club history.Respected United fan and United We Stand fanzine editor Andy Mitten, who interviewed chief executive Omar Berrada on behalf of the club last June, described the performance as "an affront to the name of Manchester United".In addition to the catastrophic nature of the performance, captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick's tactics and the inability of his coaches to spot what was going wrong.Fernandes' comments came a week after defender Lisandro Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad and - turning attention to Jason Wilcox - "more from our technical director".It painted a picture of a squad out of control, posing an immediate dilemma for the United hierarchy.Feeling it would look reactionary and impulsive to remove Carrick based on the negativity of one game, United stuck with the 45-year-old for the Bournemouth match - only for that to turn sour thanks to a performance that, arguably, was worse than the one in Italy.Fernandes played no part and was dropped to the bench. Afterwards, the Portugal star liked an Instagram post which included the caption: "Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care".Late on Sunday night, BBC Sport was led to believe a final decision to sack Carrick had not been made, and the judgement would stretch into Monday.There was no decision then, either. The United players who started against Bournemouth were given the day off but bizarrely, Fernandes and Carrick were both at Carrington. Fernandes was having pre-planned treatment while Carrick watched a closed doors Under-21s game. Also at the training ground were Berrada and Wilcox, discussing what the immediate future should look like. Sources say it is inconceivable minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family would not have been part of those discussions. It was early evening before it became clear there would be no update on Carrick's future. His arrival at Carrington at 07:30 GMT on Tuesday was a sign he would take training as normal and, along with Fernandes and several other players, Carrick signed autographs and posed for photographs with a group of fans invited to the training ground that day.Four hours later, United sources confirmed he would be in charge at Stamford Bridge.The current predicament at the club is seen as not being entirely Carrick's fault.Senior figures at the club feel United's players - a squad they think are capable of qualifying for the Champions League - are underperforming badly and should shoulder some of the blame.There does seem to be a general desire to help Carrick out. One player told BBC Sport: "The feeling is that we all want to put it right. Players, staff, everyone." It is not known if the "we" includes Fernandes, and BBC Sport has not been made aware of what, if any, conversations have taken place between the captain and his boss.Obviously, it is easier to get rid of one manager and his backroom team than an entire squad of players - and if results do not turn around, Carrick will pay the price.One former senior United official told BBC Sport: "Ordinarily, Michael would have gone. The last two performances were unacceptable and team discipline is broken. Not doing it is fascinating and risky."Cynics may argue the main reason Carrick is still in a job is because of the inability to secure a replacement before the Chelsea game. Additionally, some of the coaches current Under-18s boss Darren Fletcher called on to help him during his spell as interim manager in January are now part of the senior set-up.As highlighted by BBC Sport on Monday, Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann were among the options explored by United as they weighed up whether to make a change. Any decision to appoint Howe would trigger a multi-million pound compensation payment from his former club Newcastle. Some observers think compensation payments may be a factor in United's reluctance to make a change, given the sums that have previously gone on hiring and firing coaches.BBC Sport has also been told former Chelsea boss Antonio Conte is willing to have a conversation about the job, although there has been no direct contact.That trio are all out of work - as is Kieran McKenna, who worked with Carrick as part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at United and then left for Ipswich.Aston Villa's Unai Emery also has strong backing at United, but the club are realistic about their chances of tempting the Spaniard from Villa Park.Wilcox's future has also come under intense scrutiny.One source close to United feels it is inevitable the former Blackburn and Leeds player will eventually lose his job if a third managerial change in as many seasons is made.There is sympathy with Wilcox, who did not set the summer transfer budget. Others say Ratcliffe has provided significant funds for transfers since he took charge of football affairs in early 2024, as well as injecting £300m of his own money into the club.While disgruntled fans may point to the recruitment of teams such as Brentford and Brighton as proof good players can be signed without paying astronomical fees, options for bigger clubs such as United were said to be scarce during the summer window.Nevertheless, it has never been explained why it was decided to focus on bolstering the midfield last summer, rather than address clear personnel issues at left-back and central striker. Injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko have made that issue even more acute.Another senior figure in the game told BBC Sport both Wilcox and Berrada may be vulnerable, suggesting Ratcliffe could be considering a wider overhaul of senior staff.For now, though, minds are focused on Stamford Bridge, with Carrick due to speak to the media on Thursday.

schema.headline: Michael Carrick: Why Man Utd are sticking with under-pressure manager - for now

title: Anti-social behaviour by neighbours has been 'hell', tenant says
description: For seven years James Daniel has been living next to successive "nightmare neighbours". Despite numerous complaints to various agencies, including his
body: For seven years James Daniel has been living next to successive "nightmare neighbours". Despite numerous complaints to various agencies, including his housing association, he said his situation had not improved. It comes as new data from the Housing Ombudsman showed a rise over five years in the number of complaints upheld about social landlords' handling of anti-social behaviour.While Devon and Cornwall Police has increased the number of closure orders placed on residential properties, housing associations report that dealing with anti-social behaviour can be a complex issue and requires working closely with other agencies. Daniel said he had spent years reporting the alleged anti-social behaviour and collecting evidence, including security camera and mobile phone footage, which he passed on to the police, North Devon Homes and now the BBC. The videos he shared with the BBC showed knives being thrown from a window, an altercation outside his house and a neighbour appearing to make gun gestures at his security camera.Other footage showed a previous tenant shouting at Daniel and other residents, as well as throwing bags of rubbish and a dust pan brush."Living next door to anti-social behaviour has been hell to be honest, absolute hell," said Daniel.New data showed the Housing Ombudsman upheld almost four times as many complaints relating to social landlords' handling of anti-social behaviour reports than five years ago.In the 2021-2022 financial year, the ombudsman found failings in 159 incidents compared with 609 in 2025–26.Ric Blakeway, the Housing Ombudsman at the time, said there were a number of "consistent reasons" why the maladministration rate - or uphold rate - had increased."It's poor communication, it's poor record keeping, it's not using the tools that landlords should use - such as doing a risk assessment or producing an action plan - and that is a consistent reason that we would uphold a case," he explained."Where we don't uphold it though, I think you see the kind of opposite of that."Easier access to the ombudsman service and greater awareness of housing rights were among the drivers Blakeway believed had led to a rise in casework.Blakeway said his teams had seen cases where residents had been making themselves "in effect homeless" by sleeping in cars to escape the anti-social behaviour.In West Cornwall, neighbours said closure orders on two properties in the same street had been effective. Melanie, whose surname we are not using, said residents had been "living in fear" before one neighbour, who was accused of waving a sword, was removed. "You shouldn't have to live like that these days," she said.At another property, PC James Tompson said officers spent weeks gathering evidence of drug use, fighting and anti-social behaviour linked to the address.In April, Daniel's neighbour was convicted of assaulting another resident and a month later was charged with allegedly harassing him.Daniel said victims of anti-social behaviour, particularly in social housing, needed support from agencies in a "more joined up approach"."For me, it's about highlighting the system is broken," he said."All the agencies are involved but actually it seems nobody's talking to each other, and nobody knows what's going on."He said he no longer felt safe at home and that it was becoming "impossible to get any support" for those affected by anti-social behaviour."It's got to the point where actually the house that I love, I don't love anymore," he added.

schema.headline: Anti-social behaviour by neighbours has been 'hell', tenant says

title: Bahamas: King Charles acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
description: King Charles has arrived in the Bahamas for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean - the first time he has visited the region as monarch.The King, wearing s
body: King Charles has arrived in the Bahamas for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean - the first time he has visited the region as monarch.The King, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was given a ceremonial welcome at the airport before attending a youth rally.Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during the visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.Appearing at his first engagement, he told young people it is "only right" to "acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past".Upon arriving on the island, he met island's Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour on the runway.The King was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended the island's independence celebrations as Prince of Wales in 1973.During his speech, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".He went on to call on the young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into his schedule in all three countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region". For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity. He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.CHOGM is a biennial summit which brings together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

schema.headline: Bahamas: King Charles acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins

title: Nanotyrannus: Dinosaur skeleton sells for $47.3m in New York auction
description: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (£35.5m).Nic
body: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (£35.5m).Nicknamed Jodi, the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton was auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.The Late Cretaceous carnivore was expected to fetch at least $9m when it went under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed Gus, for a record $50.1m in July.The sale has reignited debate in the scientific community over whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately or displayed publicly.Sotheby's described Jodi as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science". The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.The identify of the buyer, who won after a thrilling 12 minutes of auction bidding between six interested parties, has not been disclosed.It becomes the second-most valuable dinosaur fossil ever sold, behind Gus. The third-most valuable was a Stegosaurus named Apex, which was sold by Sotheby's in July 2024 for $44.6m.Megan Jacobs, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex"."But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jacobs said.Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.Jodi was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hell Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from Jodi in 2006.The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.The auction of Jodi comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.Researchers told the BBC after the sale of Gus that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning"."I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."He said at the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.Responding to Tuesday's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that Jodi could disappear from public view. "We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.But Jacobs told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens."I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

schema.headline: Nanotyrannus: Dinosaur skeleton sells for $47.3m in New York auction

title: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJake HortonBBC VerifyPresident Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJake HortonBBC VerifyPresident Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.How has Trump tried to change postal voting?For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.The majority of states allow, external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.What is the SAVE America Act and what would it do?Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictionsHowever, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks, external.What does the evidence show on postal voting fraud?Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.The Brookings Institute policy research think tank, external looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.We looked back in the database, external over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association, external looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.How has Trump tried to change voter ID rules?Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Millions of people have already voted early in the US midterm electionsCritics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID."We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.Can illegal immigrants really vote in the US election?A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws."When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice, external.What does the evidence show on non-citizens voting?Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.A 2026 analysis by Reuters, external of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction."The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institute."There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."What about non-citizens registered on voter rolls?Trump has also pushed for states to use a federal database - the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) database - to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens and remove them from voter rolls.The tool has access to information about naturalised citizens and non-citizens who have contacted the federal government previously. It was launched in the 1980s to help government agencies verify individuals' eligibility for government benefits based on their immigration status.Critics have questioned the reliability of using the data to remove people from voter rolls as they say it could be outdated and include people who have since become US citizens - but the US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using it this way.US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenshipImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Every US state allows some postal voting and 29% of voters cast a ballot that way in the 2024 presidential election"Federal databases can be invaluable to states trying to update their voter rolls so long as their limitations are understood," says Olson. "So part of the Trump plan which requires the sharing of information is positive, even if the second part to require states to treat the database contents as reliable despite their continuing evident gaps and inaccuracies is bad."The use of the programme by individual states is voluntary, and from those who have used it recently the number of non-citizens detected has been small.In Georgia, after an audit of the state's voter rolls, 432 possible non-citizens were identified, external on its voter rolls over 30 years.The Department of Homeland Security provided Nevada with a list of 185 names which it claimed identified non-citizens who had been improperly allowed to register to vote, but state officials found that they were all in fact citizens., externalThe White House has pointed to a case in New Jersey, where this summer a software glitch in the state's drivers licensing department registered about 6,600 non-citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. State officials have said fewer than 400 cast ballots and they have all now been removed from the system.The US Justice Department requested that California doesn't count 20,000 postal ballots ahead of the midterms from people it claims are "likely non-citizen registrants" - but that request has been rejected by an appeals court.Out of that 20,000, it has charged 28 people, external who the department says are non-citizens who had illegally registered to vote.

schema.headline: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increases
description: The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years,
body: The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living."The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC: "Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27.That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to £13.20, the Times said.Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job."Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."The government has also announced a number of measures, including removing import taxes on some food and ending the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments.It says removing tariffs from 100 food items could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June."We're not going to say it is everything," Reynolds told the BBC, but taken alongside the changes implemented in the summer on goods such as pasta, fruit juice and tuna, he said it would save around £500m a year.Other measures the government announced on Tuesday included:Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above thatAllowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the periodAnd rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easierSpeaking to the BBC's Newscast, Healey said: "None of this is going to change the world. But if it helps around the margins and its action the government can take, then I want try and fix it."The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. The 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes:Baked beansGarlicGherkinsChocolate-coated wafers and wafflesBoiled sweetsToffees, caramels and similar sweetsCitrus jams, marmalades and pastesThroat pastilles and cough dropsPlant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seedKeroseneFertilisersThe government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targeted at households that rely on heating oil.The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed.A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas.Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take."But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs."The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

schema.headline: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increases

title: My husband's death was hard enough - then came the admin
description: Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John meticulously planned the handover of household admin before his deathByJennifer MeierhansLouisa Nicoll
body: Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John meticulously planned the handover of household admin before his deathByJennifer MeierhansLouisa Nicoll knew her husband John was going to die about a year before it happened. The couple used the time to make memories with their children, James and Amy, and John meticulously organised their paperwork.But despite him asking for accounts to be switched to Louisa's name, she still received post addressed to him after his death. In one letter from their energy provider, it said: "Sorry you're leaving us. Is there anything we can do to make you stay?""I felt utterly exhausted, overwhelmed, frustrated and angry because of those experiences," she told BBC's Morning Live.Louisa now campaigns for changes in the way companies deal with admin after someone dies and offers advice on how talking about death before it happens can help families cope afterwards.Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, After their father's death, James and Amy still received texts from their mobile phone provider that read "Hi, John"  John was 50 and working as a police surveillance trainer when he was diagnosed with cancer. Louisa had a career in palliative care nursing and was a ward manager in a hospice. John underwent nine major surgeries and four rounds of chemotherapy - working full-time through it all."He absolutely loved working with his supportive police colleagues, and he cherished everyday family life and spending time with our friends," says Louisa.When further surgery was no longer an option, palliative chemotherapy was offered. Following many discussions, John decided to focus on making memories as a husband, dad and friend rather than spending his final months as a patient."He made a lovely speech at Amy's 18th birthday," she says. "We visited family in Scotland and had planned a family holiday to Greece - but Covid hit and we had a Greek night at home instead." The couple had a party for Louisa's 50th and their 25th wedding anniversary.Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John wrote Louisa an 18-page document called "things to make you smile"In the background, John was busy compiling a handover of the household admin."He even wrote a plan for me titled 'things you need to know', packed with every household account, insurance renewal and MOT dates," she says.He had emailed their energy provider saying he would like Louisa to take over as the account holder due to his terminal diagnosis.But instead, she was added as an additional name and had to close and reopen the account."I thought I was prepared for John's death but the reality was so much harder than I could ever have imagined. He really was the other half of me. So when I had to face the death admin, I felt so vulnerable without him beside me."James and Amy's mobile phone contracts were in John's name, too. They were asked to take his death certificate into a store but still received texts that read "Hi, John"."I'm sure nobody's doing this intentionally... but these companies could just get their bereavement services at a level that is not going to cause undue distress," says Louisa. "There should be a standardised practice."Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, Louisa urges families regardless of age to have conversations and make end-of-life plans Sarah Middlemiss, policy campaigns manager at end-of-life charity Marie Curie, tells Morning Live admin tasks can be particularly difficult when you are grieving."And because every company does things in a slightly different way and requires slightly different things, it can be really, really overwhelming," she says."Proper training on how to deal with people who are grieving or who are terminally ill in a really sensitive and timely manner would go a really long way."Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John and Louisa at a family wedding before his diagnosisLouisa gives talks at events to encourage people to talk about death in advance."We plan for every major event in life - weddings, pregnancy, career changes, retirement, even our meals each day - yet most people leave the end of life completely to chance," she says."Our families end up trapped in a crisis - guessing our wishes in the back of an ambulance or a chaotic A&E department."She says she and John had those "hard but important conversations" long before they needed them.Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, Louisa says John kept his sense of humour and personality throughout his treatmentJohn died peacefully at home in August 2020, just one day after their 26th wedding anniversary."Before he died, we spoke about what I would do for work after he died. He said, 'I think you'll tell our story, and show people that it is possible to live well when faced with dying.' And that is what I'm trying to do."How to get your affairs in orderGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: My husband's death was hard enough - then came the admin
